Neurology · published research

Cerebral palsy

A small randomized study in children with spastic diplegia reported less pain, greater muscle power, and lower blood lactate after PBM. Older controlled reports describe reduced myotonia, while the bone study measured markers rather than demonstrating fewer fractures.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small randomized study in children with spastic diplegia reported less pain, greater muscle power, and lower blood lactate after PBM. Older controlled reports describe reduced myotonia, while the bone study measured markers rather than demonstrating fewer fractures.

Summary of the Evidence

The direct cerebral-palsy category contains five unique titles: three human primary publications, one review, and one trial protocol. The human studies include a 40-child randomized study, a 73-person non-randomized controlled study, and an uncontrolled 20-person report. One additional publication in the database’s cerebral-palsy bone category is mapped narrowly because it treats children with severe cerebral palsy and measures bone metabolism. A later bone-metabolism paper from the same research group appears to report related outcomes from that cohort and is not counted as another independent study.

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized study of 40 children with spastic diplegia, one month of laser treatment was associated with greater muscle power, lower blood lactate, and less pain than the comparison condition. These are directly measured muscle outcomes; the study does not establish broad improvement in mobility or participation (Abdelhalim et al. 2023).

An older controlled study of 73 people reported reduced myotonia and described PBM as an adjunct to intensive functional training. Because allocation was not randomized and training was part of the care, the results do not isolate the light effect. A separate 20-person uncontrolled report addressed adults with athetoid cerebral palsy.

The mapped bone study followed 25 children with severe cerebral palsy and reported changes in bone-metabolism markers after LED treatment. Its published outcomes concern markers and bone-density observations, not a controlled demonstration that PBM prevents fractures (Asagai et al. 2014 Asagai et al. 2015).

Animal evidence

No animal experiment is classified in the direct cerebral-palsy or mapped bone category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study is classified for cerebral palsy in these categories.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The 2023 randomized study used continuous 810 nm near-infrared laser light, 200 mW, and 30 J at each of 18 muscle points, five times per week for one month. The database reports 5.49 W/cm² irradiance and 164.85 J/cm² fluence; these are the study’s reported dosimetry, not a validated target dose. The 2005 study used 810 nm laser treatment on acupuncture points alongside training. The mapped bone study used broad 400–700 nm visible LED light at very low reported irradiance. These targets and protocols address different outcomes, and no dose-finding comparison identifies an optimal setting.

Interpretation

The randomized trial reports favorable changes in pain, muscle power, and blood lactate in children with spastic diplegia. The older controlled report also describes reduced myotonia during training, while the bone study reports marker changes rather than proven fracture prevention. The clinical findings support further testing of these specific muscle outcomes; they do not yet establish broad motor gains or skeletal protection.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term muscle fatigue, pain, and power outcomes in children with spastic diplegia Very low for broad motor function or fracture prevention
Publications and recordsDirect category: 5 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A randomized study in children with spastic diplegia reported improved pain and muscle power with lower blood lactate, and an older controlled study reported reduced myotonia during functional training. These results support specific short-term muscle outcomes rather than a general motor benefit. Replicated blinded trials with standardized doses and functional follow-up would strengthen the rating; fracture prevention needs direct fracture outcomes.
